title: Keith Richards Brings His Blues Grit to the Grand Theft Auto VI Soundtrack
summary: Keith Richards has been playing guitar for more than 60 years, but he's still finding new ways to surprise fans. The Rolling Stones legend recorded his own version of "Bright Lights, Big City," a 1961 blues song by Jimmy Reed, for Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album. The soundtrack — 34 songs meant to capture the "electric energy" of the game's fictional Vice City and Leonida — drops November 19. Reed's original had a medium tempo, with a swinging guitar line and a searing harmonica solo. Richards plays the guitar with more force and sings with a trembling quiver that owes a debt to Reed's style, adding something like a Mississippi-via-Dartford drawl. Where Reed had a harmonica solo, Richards plays straight through to the fade. There's no word on when or where Richards recorded the track — maybe during sessions for the Stones' recent albums Foreign Tongues or Hackney Diamonds. Either way, he's been on a roll. Rolling Stone praised his Hackney Diamonds song "Tell Me Straight," calling it "as taut as the rest of the album," and described Foreign Tongues' "Some of Us" as "a moving declaration of devotion" that showed "deep emotion and vulnerability." The Stones have no 2026 touring plans, but Richards told Uncut he could see the band doing a residency somewhere. "It's the traveling that takes it out of you," he said. "But I do see the possibility of us doing a residency somewhere. Wherever it is, London, New York, Paris, anywhere. I'll play Rome!" At 82, Richards keeps adding to a career that started in 1962. Not bad for a guy who once said he'd rather be dead than play "Satisfaction" again.
why_it_matters: It shows how music keeps moving between generations and media: a blues song from 1961 reaches millions of teenagers through a video game, while an 82-year-old guitarist keeps recording — evidence that video games now function as a major music platform and that older artists can stay culturally relevant by adapting to them.

background_read: The Rolling Stones (the British rock band formed in London in the early 1960s) took their name from a Muddy Waters blues song, 'Rollin' Stone.' Their first albums were packed with covers of American blues artists, so Keith Richards returning to a Jimmy Reed song more than sixty years later is something of a homecoming.

Jimmy Reed (an American blues singer and guitarist from Mississippi who recorded in Chicago) released 'Bright Lights, Big City' in 1961, and it became one of his best-known songs. His simple, repeating guitar riffs and relaxed singing made his records a training ground for young British groups in the 1960s, who learned American blues from imported records and copied them closely.

Video games have become a major way people discover music. Grand Theft Auto (a series made by the company Rockstar Games) has used in-game radio stations as a selling point since the early 2000s, mixing famous hits with obscure tracks, and Grand Theft Auto VI is set in the fictional state of Leonida and its Vice City, a stand-in for Miami.

Keith Richards (born in Dartford, England, in the 1940s — the town the article name-checks in 'Mississippi-via-Dartford drawl') has been the Stones' guitarist and main co-writer for over six decades and has continued releasing music and appearing live long past the age when most rock stars retire.

perspectives.description: Fans get an unexpected cross-generation moment: a Rolling Stones legend reworking a blues classic that most young players only know second-hand. Richards' continued output at 82, and Rolling Stone's praise for his recent work, suggest an artist still growing rather than repeating himself.

Purists may argue that attaching a 1961 blues song to a huge commercial game soundtrack turns a piece of Black American musical history into marketing for a blockbuster product. Others note the irony of celebrating Richards' blues cover while the original artists often earned far less.

The Stones built their career on covering American blues, and their very name comes from a Muddy Waters song — so a Jimmy Reed cover is a sixty-year-old cycle repeating itself. The newer twist is the platform: in-game radio has replaced radio airplay as a way teenagers stumble onto old songs.

The open questions are whether the Stones will actually announce a residency, and whether game albums keep pushing older artists into new audiences. If the cross-over works commercially, more legacy acts are likely to follow Richards into soundtracks aimed at players half a century younger.
